frameworks.name: Opportunity Prioritization Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-tier system for selecting which business opportunities to pursue: first, activities requiring no new skills or effort; second, activities requiring effort but no new skills; third, activities requiring new skills with highest leverage payoff.

frameworks.name: Risk-Adjusted Return Analysis
frameworks.definition: Comparing opportunities not by eliminating risk, but by normalizing risk across different options using risk-adjusted return metrics to evaluate relative safety rather than absolute safety.

frameworks.name: Investor Decision Making as Universal Principle
frameworks.definition: The investor mindset—quantified decision-making with scoreboard-validated track records—applies beyond finance to personal life decisions and provides superior frameworks for evaluating options.

claims.text: Every investment opportunity has reasons to reject it, because no opportunity is risk-free; even US Treasury bonds carry risk if the US economy collapses. The solution is not to seek risk-free opportunities but to compare risk-adjusted returns across options.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Eliminating risk from evaluation criteria makes all opportunities appear equally risky; comparing risk-adjusted returns instead allows rational prioritization.

claims.text: Risk-adjusted return is one of the most important skillsets for entrepreneurs, because fundamentally business is betting—every day founders bet time and money against unlimited opportunities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Entrepreneurs allocate limited resources (time, capital) across unlimited opportunities; skill at normalizing and comparing risks determines which bets succeed.

claims.text: When evaluating which business opportunities to pursue, start by identifying activities requiring no new skills and minimal new effort; once those are exhausted, pursue activities requiring more effort but still no new skills; only then learn new skills, prioritizing by leverage (maximum output for minimum input).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Opportunities requiring existing skills complete fastest and compound immediately, freeing capacity for leverage-generating skill acquisition; this sequence minimizes failure risk from dependency on new unproven skills.
bounded_by: Does not prescribe learning skills in parallel
Assumes founder prefers deterministic wins before experimental ones

claims.text: The investor mindset—scoreboard-validated decision-making—is universally applicable to personal life decisions (e.g., learning salsa vs. coding) not just financial investment, because investors have undeniable track records proving their decision-making quality while most other advisors lack measurable scoreboards.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A scoreboard (quantified success metrics over time) objectively validates decision-making quality; sources with proven scorecards are more reliable than equally confident but unvalidated advisors.
bounded_by: Applies only to decisions where the advisor has a measurable track record
Requires the decision domain to be quantifiable

claims.text: Ray Dalio's Principles book became a bestseller despite 99.9% of readers not being investors or at Dalio's level, because the principles of quantified good decision-making are universally applicable, not domain-specific.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: Uber is cited as a big-win investment that seemed like a terrible idea on the surface—'strangers pick up girls who are 16 and drive them to their friends' houses'—but worked because a mutual rating system reduced the actual risk below the perceived risk. This illustrates how opportunities with bounded downside but unbounded upside can appear risky until you identify the mechanism that caps the downside.

The metaphor of opportunity selection as rating potential romantic partners ('there's unlimited women in the red dress...some fours and some sixes and some eights') illustrates how both the attractiveness of the opportunity (the rating) and the risk factors (how unpredictable or unstable) must be evaluated in parallel, not sequentially.

practices.text: Document and quantify your decision-making track record to build a scoreboard that validates (or invalidates) the quality of your advice, making your decision-making framework trustworthy to others.
When sorting through opportunities, explicitly separate the evaluation into two distinct questions: how good is the opportunity (the rating), and how unpredictable or risky is it (the risk factors).
